Running example · Updated Fri Nov 20

Fernhill Software

One fictional project, built alongside yours. Each draft is posted as yours comes due, and revised in the open when the evidence calls for it.

The decision

Fernhill Software is a fictional business-software firm with about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams. It promotes its strongest engineers into management, where some struggle.

As AI coding tools arrive, a leader proposes hiring professional managers for people skill, making engineer-managers technical leads, and using AI to fill managers’ technical gaps. Should Fernhill make the change?

How the model evolves

Each version makes its model explicit, tests what it can, and uses what it learns to ask a better question. Highlighted boxes mark an idea or design feature in that step.

Choose a version or play the sequence. On a small screen, use the figure’s larger view to read its labels.

Version 1 · The enthusiast's model

Starting model · professional management and AI

The model. People skill in the manager’s chair raises delivery, and AI covers the technical gap.

What we learned. The manager and AI changed together. Other things changed too. Before and after alone could not separate their effects. What version 1 taught us

What changed next. Assign teams by lot, rate difficulty before the work, and model where technical questions go. Explore version 2

Version 2 · The trial designer's model

New in this diagram · assignment by lot, planning difficulty, escalations and waits

The model. A lot sets the structure and AI. Difficulty shapes escalations, which can queue into a wait.

What we learned. The arms differed on hard work, and a few long waits coincided with low delivery. The trial compared the arms, but it did not measure the manager–lead relationship. What version 2 taught us

What changed next. Draw the handoff, measure the relationship, and use a second lot for HR’s response. Explore version 3

Version 3 · The gold standard

New in this diagram · the manager–lead relationship and HR feedback

The model. Every escalation crosses the manager–lead relationship. Results and HR can reshape that relationship.

What the data can tell us. The relationship score and delivery can move together without the score causing delivery. Results feed back into the relationship, and other factors can affect both.

What the design adds. A monthly pulse and overrides measure aspects of the relationship, while pair records identify the people involved. A second lot compares HR acting with scores sealed. The relationship itself was not assigned by lot. Explore version 3 results · Read the diagrams

What evolves

Each version asks what the evidence can support, then changes the model or the design in response. Open the versions to follow the reasoning, results and limits.

VersionThe modelEvidence and response
Version 1People skill and AI are expected to raise delivery.Before and after cannot separate management, AI and other changes.
Version 2A lot separates AI and structure. The model adds difficulty, escalations and waits.Long waits and weak hard-quarter delivery prompted a closer look at the manager–lead handoff.
Version 3The model adds the manager–lead relationship and how it changes.Measure the relationship and test HR’s response. A relationship score alone cannot establish cause.
